title: The CRA and you
blurb: Who collects tax, your SIN, how the system began and where the money goes.

levels.title: What the CRA does
learn: Say what the CRA collects, and for whom.
Name the money it pays out as benefits and credits.

cards.text: The Canada Revenue Agency, or CRA, runs tax laws for the federal government and for most provinces and territories. A tax law is a rule about who pays tax and how much.

image.alt: A stone office building with a blank flag and a desk of blank forms

cards.text: In Alberta, the CRA collects personal income tax together with federal income tax. So an Alberta taxpayer deals with the CRA for both.

image.alt: A blank province map with gold discs and a magnifying glass

cards.text: Canada's system relies on each person filing their own return every year. A return is the form that reports your income and works out your tax.

image.alt: A desk with a blank form, a pen, gold discs and a mug of tea

cards.text: The CRA also pays money out. It runs benefit and incentive programs through the tax system. A benefit is a payment to people who qualify.

image.alt: A mailbox with gold discs spilling onto snow and a blank envelope

cards.text: One benefit is the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, once called the GST/HST credit. It is paid every three months to eligible people.
To continue to receive benefit and credit payments, people must update their information with the CRA each year. They do this by filing their income tax and benefit return.

image.alt: A balance scale with a gold disc on each tray and a blank document

levels.title: Your SIN
learn: Say what a SIN is and how to apply for one.
Say who may ask for it and why you guard it.

cards.text: A Social Insurance Number, or SIN, is a nine-digit number you need to work in Canada and to use government programs and benefits. Service Canada issues it.

image.alt: A blank card beside a closed passport cover and a pen on a desk

cards.text: You can apply for a SIN online, by mail, or in person. There is no fee. Anyone 12 years or older can apply for their own SIN.

image.alt: A laptop, a sealed envelope and a small counter with a blank sign

cards.text: To apply, you give the documents the application asks for. One is a birth certificate issued by a vital statistics agency. The list also includes a passport, a provincial or territorial ID card or driver's licence, and other Canadian government ID.

figure.title: Papers for a SIN application
rows: Driver's licence or provincial ID card

cards.text: Employers need your SIN to report your income for tax and social benefits. Financial institutions need your SIN to report income like interest and dividends. Only provide your SIN when the law requires it.

image.alt: A blank clipboard and pay slips with a small bank counter behind

cards.text: Your confirmation of SIN letter and your SIN card are not identity documents. Do not show them to prove who you are.

image.alt: A blank card in a sleeve beside a passport and a licence card

cards.text: Guard your SIN. It is private, and it is illegal for anyone else to use it. Protecting it protects you from fraud and identity theft. Identity theft is when someone uses your details to pretend to be you.

image.alt: A brass padlock on a wooden box with a key on a hook

levels.title: How it began, where it goes
learn: Say when federal income tax began and why.
Read the main sources and uses of federal money.

cards.text: Canada's federal income tax began in 1917, under the Income War Tax Act. An income tax is a tax on the money people earn.

image.alt: An old desk with a blank ledger, inkwell and quill

cards.text: It began as a temporary measure to pay for the war. Today each person still files a return every year.

image.alt: A sand timer on blank sheets beside a row of gold discs

cards.text: Each year the government reports what it took in and spent. In 2025-26, personal income tax brought in more than the GST. Amounts are in millions of dollars.
In 2025-26 the federal government spent $565.7 billion. These eight lines add up to $547.8 billion, which is less than the total, so some spending is not listed.

figure.title: Federal spending, 2025-26
rows: Federal transfer support for health and social programs

cards.text: Each bar shows one category as a share of all $565.7 billion spent. Other direct program expenses is the biggest line, at 23.2 percent.
The government spent $565.7 billion and took in $526.4 billion. That is $39.3 billion more spent than collected. These are federal numbers for one year, 2025-26.

image.alt: A balance scale tipped toward a tall stack of gold discs
